chapter: Jess Stacy, Goodman and New York characters
title: Charles Edward Smith and the Russian critic prank
summary: Hodes tells how Condon invented a Russian critic to deflate Charles Edward Smith at Julius' Bar.

story.theme_name: Band pranks, jokes and gigs gone wrong
story.community_name: Pranks, practical jokes and band humor

blocks.x: Charles Edward Smith at that time in our period in New York was getting some acclaim as a writer.
He was writing for Esquire; as was Leonard.
Right, and the book that he wrote, or part of a book.

And he was also taking a little weight on in his head, where he was getting a little heavy to be around. And after all, we all hung out at Julius' Bar and Grill, which was around the corner of Nick's. And that's where we got our mail, it was our country store, it was our library, this was it. Eddie Condon would wheel his baby up and leave her outside in the buggy and he'd go inside. And this is where we lived, part of the day.

And Charles Edward hung out there, which was getting to be a pain in the ass to Eddie. And Eddie's got a good mind, so he started thinking, what are you going to do about it? So he set this up. And Smith came in one night, and he introduced this guy, who looked like a Russian. Might have looked a little like Kenny Davern with a moustache, and a little hat. "This is Vladimir Steenevitz, a great Russian jazz critic. And this is Charles Edwards Smith, great American writer, jazz critic. Oh, glad to know you. And the Russian says to him, what do you play? And Smith says, I don't play nothing." And the Russian looks at him and says, in Russia, we
And that was it. From then on, we got along very well with Smith. He got the point after awhile, because we broke up, the whole bar broke up and they just -- it was just too much.
